maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
This provision will
apply not only to dealers, but also to any persons who have packages to send. If the suggestion of my hon. friend were carried out, the position would be this: if I should happen to have occasion to send a package that might contain liquor to my hon. friend or to any one else, unless I had some method of indelibly labelling my particular package

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: It is an easy matter for a dealer; a printing iron would burn the name into the package.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.

speechtext: Amendment agreed to.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I should like to make an inquiry of the minister as to the operation of this legislation in a province where there is legislation along this line which is not province-wide. In my province the , Scott Act is in operation in some counties, and there is also-in operation in some parts of the province a measure which is not called a prohibitory measure-it is called the Liquor Act-but which contemplates licensing under certain conditions which are so onerous that they are practically pro-

hibitive. Would the provisions of my hon. friend's measure be operative in a province where there is not in existence a provincewide act; where there is no measure declaratory of the prohibition principle, though the measures in operation may be prohibitory in effect?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
This Act would not
operate as regards transportation from one placS in the province into another place in the province. If a man sends liquor into a province which is only partially under prohibition, knowing that it is going to be taken into the prohibitory places or dealt with in the prohibitory places, I think he would come under the provisions of this Act. It is intended that he should, and I think the wording brings him under it. I have in contemplation, so far as transportation within the provinces is concerned, one or two small amendments to the Canada Temperance Act, which I will put in a separate Bill so that it may form part of the Canada Temperance Act. The purpose is to deal with transportation from places under the Canada Temperance Act into other parts of the provinces that may be under provincial law. The Canada Temperance Act already safeguards those portions of provinces that are under the Canada Temperance Act, but I propose extending that provision so as to make it, following the principle of this Bill, protect other portions of a province from the sending of liquor from those parts under the Canada Temperance Act to be used in violation of a provincial law.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
When the liquor
comes in, in order to make the bringing in an offence under this Act, the knowledge to be possessed by the consignee is that the liquor is being imported for the purpose of being sold in contravention of the Act. Where you have no provincial legislation prohibiting the use of liquor as a beverage, it is open to the person who desires to do so to import liquor for his own use; this Act would not apply in such a case?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: It is proposed to protect the existing law, but not to make prohibitions against things which the province itself tolerates.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I desire to draw the minister's attention to a peculiar situation that has arisen in some counties in Ontario. The county of Perth has passed the Scott Act or Canada Temperance Act, which will come into force on the 1st of May next.
The Provincial Government are about putting through an Act which will come into force on the 16th of September. There will !be two prohibitory Acts, therefore, affecting the same county, and providing different pains and penalties for the same offence. I have been requested to ask the minister to consider legislation either repealing the Scott Act or postponing the operation of it in such a county until such time as the provincial legislation becomes effective.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
As regards the two systems of legislation coming into effect in the same county, as I understand it, the fact that the Canada Temperance Act is in force in the county will exclude the applicability of any provincial law. Under the decisions of the Privy Council, holding that there was power in the Dominion to deal with the subject from its point of view and in the provinces to deal with it from their point of view, it. is recognized that where the Dominion Parliament exercises its power of legislation with regard to the subject, and where a law enacted by the Dominion Parliament is in force in any particular province, that law ousts the power of a Provincial Legislature and therefore excludes the application of provincial law. Applying that to the particular case mentioned, as I understand it, the proposed Ontario prohibition law will not be effective in these counties in Ontario in wdiich the Canada Temperance Act is in force, so that there will be no question of both laws being in force within the same territory. As to the suggestion that we should defer the application of the Canada Temperance Act in the particular county mentioned, I should be glad to give it consideration. But I would point out that the people to whom the matter was submitted to vote upon voted that the Canada Temperance Act should go into foroe on the first of May next. Acting upon that vote, as the Act provides, the Governor in Council issued a proclamation accordingly. At first glance, it seems to me that it would hardly be the proper thing, in face of that vote of the people of the county to have the Act come into force on the 1st of May next, for this Parliament to intervene and say that it should not come into force until a later period. There would be much force in the suggestion if the county were at some period to find itself under both laws, but, inasmuch as the Canada Temperance Act will remain in force in the county for the next three years,

if I remember rightly, I am not disposed to think, at all events without further consideration, that we should interfere to prevent the vote of the people taken under that Act from producing the effect provided for by that Act. I may say, however, as I said a few moments ago, that one or two little amendments will be made in another Bill relating to the Canada Temperance Act, and when we come to deal with that Bill, I will be glad to give consideration to what the hon. gentleman suggests.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: In this particular county you have created a peculiar anomaly. You have local option in .certain townships, the Scott Act for the whole county, provincial prohibition, and a Dominion Act in aid. What are the poor people to do with all these laws which have different provisions and different penalties? Are you going to burden them with five laws where one would do? It is said that the Ontario law will allow the sale of beer containing a certain percentage of intoxicant, so that you will have the anomaly of the province of Ontario being able, to sell beer-

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext: Except in a county under the Canada Temperance Act.

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I have said that I shall be glad to give it consideration.
Section 2 agreed to.
On section 3-place of prosecution:

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
In my view this clause may lead to trouble. The minister is, of
course, aware that all kinds of devices will be resorted to evade the provisions of this Bill; that has been the experience in the past in regard to legislation of this nature. The provision here is that the prosecution for the offence may be brought and carried on-
-in the city, town or other place from which any intoxicating liquor is sent, shipped, taken or carried as aforesaid, or in the city, town or other place to or into which such intoxicating liquor is so sent, shipped, taken, brought, carried or imported.
It would be very easy to evade that section by shipping the liquor into some place where there was no court or magistrate. It might be sent to some point where there would not be any possibility of complying with this provision. I think it would be better to redraft that section. I think the insertion of the words "in the province" would cover the case. As the section stands just now, it does not, in my opinion, cover it. I have looked at the Inland Revenue Act, and I find the following language used there in regard to the place of prosecution:
Every offence against this Act shall be deemed to have been committed, and every cause or complaint under this Act, shall be deemed to have arisen either in the place in which it actually was committed or arose, or in any place in which the person charged or complained against happens to be.
That covers everything.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.
speechtext:
I doubt very much
whether, in any of our provinces, you will find a place which has no court having jurisdiction in that place, and if there be a court which has jurisdiction in that place, a prosecution may be brought before it. The word "place " was used-I bee it is used in the Inland Revenue Act-because it was thought to be general term that would apply to a city, town, village, parish or municipality. I notice that the only difference between the provision of this Bill and that in the Inland Revenue Act, is that, apparently, under the Inland Revenue Act a man can be prosecuted in one of two places, either at the place where the offence was actually committed, or at the place where the man himself is at the time of the prosecution. If that would meet the wishes of my horn, friend I would have no objection to add a third place. We have provided that a prosecution may be taken in the place from which the liquor is sent or in the place to which it is sent. I have no objection to adding-I think it might improve the section the words "or in the place at which the party accused is."
[Hr. Doherty.!

These are the words used in the Inland Revenue Act. If you used the words " in the province " you would leave it open to the people who want to prosecute to select any place within the province to which the accused sent the liquor. Some of our provinces are very large. If liquor were shipped to a point, say, on the Gaspe coast * where there was prohibition, the party wanting to prosecute would be entitled to take the man to any district in the province of Quebec which he might select. It seems to me that that would be a hardship and an unnecessary hardship. We provide that the prosecution may be brought in the place from which the man sent the liquor or in the place where the liquor is sent to I would be quite prepared to add " or in the place in which the party accused is," or " the party accused resides," or suitable words to provide that I may prosecute a man where I find him. I think that ought to meet every requirement. .

maintopic: PROHIBITION OR RESTRICTION OF INTOXICATING LIQUORS.
subtopic: BILL IN AID OF PROVINCIAL LEGISLATION.

speechtext: This Act says you may try a man within the jurisdiction in which the offence occurred, at the place whence the goods wire sent, carried or brought, or you may try him in the place to which the goods were sent. We are giving this option to the prosecutor and thereby improving his position. It was mainly in view of the fact that we are dealing with the transmission of goods from one province into another, and the province most interested in the enforcement of this law is the province into which the goods are sent. The offence itself on the part of the sender of the goods is actually committed outside of the province into which the goods are sent and under the general rule the prosecution could not be in the province into which the goods are sent. To facilitate the enforcement of this law we have given the additional option to the party desiring to prosecute in order that he would not necessarily be called upon to go hunting his man, in so far as laying his prosecution is concerned, back to his own home but that he might be entitled to lay his charge at the court at the place to which the goods were sent. He remains free to go back to the place where the offence was committed if he thinks it more in his interests. In regard to an employee of the Intercolonial, he would be entitled to prosecute him at the place where he had committed the offence, or, in so far as this section may be applicable to the employee, to prosecute him at the place to which the goods have been brought. Mr. J. A. 0. ETHIER (Two Mountains): Mr. Speaker, in accordance with your ruling, before the House goes into Committee of Supply, I wish to call the attention of the Government to a question Which I consider of public interest, concerning complaints and grievances coming from a very worthy portion of the community, namely, the Civil Service messengers employed in the different departments of the Government. I wish to read a letter addressed to the editor of the Evening Journal and signed " Humanity," in regard to those grievances. The letter is headed, " Pictures Poverty of Government Messenger; Appeal to the Ministers," and says:
Editor Journal.-.Since a few years I have repeatedly read in the columns of the various English and French newspapers of this city, the complaints of the civil service messengers relating to their sufferings, owing to the insufficiency of their salary; but up to this day I had thought those complaints to be somewhat exaggerated, so much did I refuse to admit-and even to imagine that a Government could disregard a certain class of its servants so far as to treat them in such an injust and shameful manner.
One of those poor mesengers with whom I was conversing a few days ago made the relation of his miseries, pointing out the fact, that since 1910, the Government, as much under the Liberal Administration as under the Conservative, had been entreated by all possible means, either by deputations, by members in Parliament or through all the newspapers of this cib', to have pity on their sad condition and give them some relief. But they never paid any attention to their just solicitations.
Here is however, Mr. Editor, the situation, (related by himself) of that poor, wretched man and consequently that of all his colleagues, receiving the same salary as he:
" My salary is $500 a year, and as I had the misfbntune of having been ill in the course of the year, X have received much less than that to live with, during twelve months.
" I have been wearing the clothes with which I am clothed for three years and I have no better ones, and but for the close care of my wife, who is sewing and patching constantly you would see me in tatters. Tet those clothes bought on credit three years ago, are not all paid for.
" As long as I could get credit, the distress was less cruel, but now, the creditors seeing no

indication of any rise in my salary, refuse to advance to me any more, and even despair to ever recover what I already owe them. As a consequence, I am forced to beg from my friends, my relatives and my neighbours to make up the deficit in the pressing needs of my household.
" I have my old octogenarian parents, to whose existence I am bound to contribute; I am deprived of the possibility to accomplish that sacred duty, and the poor old ones are suffering thereby.
" We are often prevented from going to mass on Sunday, owing to the lack of the required fee.
" I have to walk an average of fifteen miles every day to attend to my work and I cannot once dispose of five cents to take a car to allay my fatigue.
" I cannot, as every citizen is called upon, and Is bound to do, contribute to the various relief funds and to other charitable organizations, being myself a beggar; I cannot, in short, fulfil my obligations towards my religion, my family and the community-I am an outcast.
" In addition to my duties as messenger, I am compelled to work assiduously as a clerk, but I am not paid one cent for that extra work.
" My wife is sick and in constant suffering, since several months, and I can't provide any medical assistance to alleviate her painful condition.
" Oftentimes in cases of sickness in my family, the doctor whom I could call without having any ready cash for him, prescribed some medicines that I could not get for want of money, and I still have in my possession several prescriptions not filled, to testify to this assertion."
I then asked this man what would be the monthly cost for the strict necessaries of his family and here is the synopsis he prepared, and which I found very modest and without exaggeration:

Now, this messenger has no children going to school, what can be the situation of the one, who, with such a salary, has three or four of an age to attend school?
Again, we must not forget the clothing, the shoes, the hats, the doctor and the medicines in case of sickness, and which are not mentioned in the above statement. Alas! If death should happen to strike at such a door, in what distressing condition would that family be situated ?	'
In what sad circumstances would this poor wretch leave his wife and children if he happened to die; his salary being insufficient to enable him to live, he is far less in a position to pay insurance premiums on his life, or contributions to any benefit societies.

And that is, Mr. Editor, the deed of a Government whose mission is to protect its subjects, a Government, having established a department to look after the welfare of the working classes in protecting them against the ambition and the injustice of the employers and contractors, and who itself turns a deaf ear to the lamentation and the pressing solicitations of its own functionaries, here in our Capital, in denying them, what they have so legitimately the right to claim: their living and nothing else.
What efficient performance of his duties can we expect from a half starved and half clad servant deprived of all indispensable comforts of living? Here I will protest most vigorously, not only in favour of the messenger, but in the name of the whole community, because the country cannot be getting the efficiency in the public service as it would get from well paid men, free of all moral and physical care.
This state of affairs is inconceivable, it is barbarous, and moreover it is a disgrace for the country, and especially when we consider that certain classes of the same service are so liberally paid and live so sumptuously.
Now come,, honourable ministers and members, stop for a moment and reflect, look from the midst of your abundance into that chilly and denuded home of your servant who is giv-mg all his time and all his intellectual and physical energy to the country, and if you have a soul and a conscience susceptible of compassion and equity, you will be eager to do justice and at the same time perform an act of humanity by granting to that neglected portion of civil employees a sufficient stipend to enable them to live and thus bring in the midst of those families, relief and happiness, peace and cheer, and you will be praised by all.
Thanking you, Mr. Editor,
I remain, with respect,

speakeroldname: Hon. ROBERT ROGERS (Minister of Public Works) :
speechtext: I have listened with attention to the remarks of the hon. member for Two Mountains. Under present circumstances, in view of existing conditions, I do not think that the messengers have very much to complain of. It is true that the law under which our messengers are engaged has been on the statute book for some time, and it provides that they shall be paid, in beginning, at the rate of $500 per annum. As my hon. friend well knows, no civil servant is taken on over the age of 36 years. Then, if an individual is not satisfied with the salary of $500 a year, of course he does not need to accept it. There are lots of applications for these various positions, and if individuals are so anxious for an increase of salary, they have an opportunity in various ways of securing that increase. To-day they can go, if they wish to do so, upon the farms in Western Canada, where they will get $40 a month and their board.
They can enlist.

If they do not like working on Western farms they can enlist and become soldiers of the King, and as such they will get even more than that. So, in view of present conditions, I do not think my hon. friend has much to support his statement. But when normal conditions return no doubt there will be some force in the argument of my hon. friend. I quite agree that any individual worthy, of employment in the Civil Service should, be entitled to receive more than $500 a year, but at the present time I could not promise my hon. friend that any change can be made. He has made a statement which I do not think is correct-that the salaries of judges have been increased in certain provinces. In no case has an increase taken place.
I understood that a Bill was presented by the Minister of Justice, in which provision was made for an increase of salaries for the judges in the province of Saskatchewan.

The hon. gentleman is in error. The salaries of judges in the province of Saskatchewan were fixed to correspond with those of judges in sister provinces of western Canada, but there have been no increases in the salaries of judges. I do not see that I can hold out any hope to my hon. friend of increasing salaries, at all events during the continuation of the war. After that, when we have had a happy restoration of the peace which we hope will come in the near future, this will be a matter for consideration, and the Civil Service will receive all the consideration they are entitled to. But at present I cannot hold out any hope of a change.

Is it the intention to spend this amount this year?
No, unless the war stops. If the hon. member could tell me that the war is going to stop this year, there are quite a number of these items that we would likely start with.
How will that make a difference?
The hon. member knows that we are spending a million dollars, or nearly so, every day on the war. If the war stops that expenditure of a million a day stops also.
But you are borrowing money for the war.

I admit that; but with the closing of the war the expenditure on war will cease, and then we shall be able or should be able to take up other expenditures in connection with items such as this that should be gone on with.

The minister knows perfectly well that, although the war may be over in a year or two years or three years,
for a very considerable period of time after its conclusion there will be the utmost necessity of husbanding the resources of Canada for the purpose of paying interest upon the war expenditure, paying pensions, and making provision for returned soldiers and wounded and disabled soldiers. A number of years will pass before we can expect normal times to return. But this is what I want to say to the minister: If he does not intend to expend this amount this year, why put it in the Estimates? I think the minister, before we proceed any further with his Estimates, ought to give us a statement of what amount of this very large appropriation of $19,815,000 in the Department of Railways and Canals, chargeable to capital, it is intended to expend during the current year. I urge this upon the minister more especially for this reason: we have a statement from the Minister of Finance that in the Estimates of $189,000,000 there is included an amount of $29,000,000 which will not be required to be expended in the public service during the current year. In connection with the Post Office Department, the Interior Department, the Department of the Secretary of State, the Department of Mines, inquiries have been made, and the statement has been given to the committee that they intend to expend practically all the money which is contained in the Estimates. I would like to know how that $29,000,000 is arrived at. We come down at last to the two great spending departments, the Department of Railways and Canals and the Department of Public Works. Unless there can be a saving of $8,000,000 or $10,000,000 in each of these departments, it is manifest that the Minister of Finance, not intentionally, but unwittingly, I am bound to assume, misled this House and the people of this country. I think it is due to the Minister of Finance that the Acting Minister of Railways and Canals, having charge of this great spending department, should tell us frankly what amount of money in .these Estimates he thinks it will not be necessary to spend during the current year.

I have confidence in Canada, and I feel sure that after the war is over, and in spite of the expenditures that have been made, Canada will be able to continue, not only to pay off the war debt, but to proceed with the construction of public works that are necessary. Canada is a great country, and I do not think that we shall go broke because of the war. I believe that the people have confidence in



the country's resources and that they will expe'ct the Government to continue, if necessary, to borrow money in order to proceed with these great vorks. So far as this item is concerned-and I understand that it is with reference to it that my hon. friend asks for information-
I am asking about all the Estimates.

If the war ends, as we all hope it will, at an early date, we will not have to borrow .$250,000,000. Perhaps the loan that we have made may carry us through the war, and if so, I think we should then proceed with the construction of the public works that we have undertaken. If the Minister of Finance can supply us with the money to go on, I would say that we should proceed with them as rapidly as possible. I cannot tell the hon. member how much of this amount we will spend, for the reason that, if the war should end within two or three months, and the Minister of Finance should be able to furnish the money, we would proceed to build whatever portion could be constructed with the money at our disposal. I do not think that the hon. member wants to strike the item out of the Estimates so that we would not be in a position to proceed to build a portion of a railway, which not only this Government desires to see built, but which 'he Government of which my hon. friend was a member intended should be proceeded with. We have included the amount in the Estimates in the hope that at an early date the war will be finished and that we may be able to proceed with the construction of the railway.
Did my hon. friend give the Minister of Finance any information as to what amounts would not be required, in all probability, during the current year?
