The hon. member knows that every session during which he has sat in this House a large portion of the Estimates submitted was not spent. There has not been a session, during the twenty-five years I have been here, in which the total amount of Estimates, as presented, was spent. In regard to the item under consideration, the hon. member will see .that we are asking for a revote of over $2,000,000 that were not spent last year, and the same thing applies to every item. The amounts placed in the Estimates are amounts which, it is estimated, will be spent, but unforeseen circumstances arise, and often it is not found necessary to spend the whole amount, or even a part of it. The Minister of Finance was perfectly justified in estimating that a certain amount of the Estimates, say $29,000,000, would not be spent, because never since Confederation has the total amount of Estimates been spent. The only answer I can give to my hon. friend is that the Minister of Finance based his Estimate on what had happened in previous years.

Then the Minister of
Finance merely guessed it?
I said that he estimated it.

Did the Minister of
Finance consult the acting Minister of Railways and Canals and go through these Estimates with him to ascertain what would likely be spent or what would not?

I think I answered that. The Minister of Finance asked me what amounts in these Estimates should be spent. My answer was that' we would spend them all if he could furnish the money. It all depends on whether the Minister of Finance can furnish the money.

The Minister of Finance is taking very effective measures to raise

money by taxing the people of this country up to the hilt. Do I understand the Acting Minister of Railways and Canals to say that he informed the Minister of Finance that he really required all this money during the current year if it could be raised? Did he put it right up to the Minister of Finance to raise the money?

No. As I said a few moments ago, while the war is on, so far as the Department of Railways and Canals is concerned, we do not wish to embarrass the Minister of Finance by asking him to raise one dollar more than is necessary. We will hold all the works we can hold, and here is one that has not been started. I would not ask the Minister of Finance to raise money to enable us to proceed with this work while the war is on.

That is getting a little nearer to what the Minister of Finance stated. This is one item, but it forms a small part of the $29,000,000 referred to by the Minister of Finance. Will the acting Minister of Railways and Canals tell us what amounts in his Estimates will be saved if the war continues during this year. I see no reasonable probability oi the war ending this year. We have heard statements in this House that when the war broke out some hon. members thought it would not last for six weeks. The hon. member for North Simcoe (Mr. Currie) said that when he left for the front everybody thought it would be over within six weeks.
I must confess that I am not one of those who dreamed of anything of the kind. Of course, I read, as everybody else read, the interview thaA the hon. the Minister of Militia and Defence (Sir Sam Hughes) gave on his return from one of his many trips to the Old Country in which he stated that England, France and Russia need not worry because Canada could put the finishing touches on Germany without the assistance of these other countries. That might be a very good indication of this Government's view as to the rapidity with which the war could be brought to an end.

Some thought there
would not be any war at all.

Even after the war
broke out. There must have been many in this country who thought there would be no war at all because we cannot find the slightest evidence of preparation being made for the war. Even gentlemen very high in the counsels of this Government 174J	.
were not aware that we could manufacture shells at the Arsenal at Quebec when the war broke out. Evidently they did not make any inquiry as to the feasibility of manufacturing munitions of war. I am-glad that the Acting Minister of Railways and Canals has gone that far, but without specifying any particular items, surely the acting minister has made up his mind as to what amounts in these Estimates can be saved provided the war should last during the coming year? It would enable us to find out what warrant the Minister of Finance had for making the statement that $29,000,000 or thereabouts of the various Estimates need not be expended.

I have not made any such
estimate as the hon. member suggests, but as we go along with each item I shall be very glad to explain it and give my opinion in regard to it. This is a new item; there has not been any work done under it as yet. As far as we are concerned I may say to the hon. gentleman that when the war broke out I was one of those who was under the impression that about six months would put an end to it.

What did the minister
base that estimate on?

On newspaper items. There were many newspapers which took that view and I was of the same opinion. But I have changed my mind in regard to that matter like other hon. gentlemen and I am now of the opinion that the war may last some little time. We can only hope that the time may not be as long as many of us fear it may be. But I trust that the war will cease and that we will be able to proceed with this work.

Of course the minister has made one statement which shows his hopefulness. He says that this country is not going to go broke and will be able to borrow money to go on with public works. Let me tell him that the members on this side of the House, and the people of the country generally, are not so much afraid that the country will go broke, to use his expression, because of the war, as because of the frightful extravagance of this Government. That is what causes great anxiety in the public mind in so far as the financial ability of the country to go on with these public works is concerned.

This is indeed a very large item, and it appears to me that, following up the policy that has been professed by

hon. gentlemen opposite, it is an item which might possibly be reduced without [DOT]any disadvantage to the country. I must confess that the remarks of the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) to-night have appealed to me with increasing force. The speech -which he made seems to be increasing in effectiveness each time he utters it in the House, and to-night, in discussing this large item of $978,000, I am prepared to confess that it does appeal to me as an item which might at least be reduced by $900,000 which would be almost %gth of the amount in the Estimates which the Minister of Finance says is not likely to be spent. I simply rise to suggest to the hon. member for St. John that if he will move to strike out this item, either wholly or in part, I shall be very much inclined to support him.

I will test my hon. friend in that. I would move that the eornmittee do not further consider the Estimates, but that you, - Mr. Chairman, leave the Chair and report to Mr. Speaker that the committee do not deem it desirable to further consider these Estimates until a reduction in the Estimates of the Department of Railways and Canals has been made by the amount of $1,000,000.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I must point out to the hon. membeT that his motion is absolutely and entirely out of order. There is no such motion recognized in the procedure of any Parliament that I have ever heard of. The hon. gentleman can move that I leave the Chair, or that the item be reduced by a certain sum. Either of these courses is open to the hon. gentleman, but outside of that I do not know of any course that is open to him.

Any motion which relates to the business that the committee has in hand is always in order. This committee may instruct you to make any report to the Speaker it chooses. My motion is that you be instructed to make a certain report to Mr. Speaker. You cannot, i't seems to me, declare the motion out of order, and, if you do, I will appeal from your decision under the rules of the House.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: I still adhere to my decision.
Then I appeal from your decision.

Does not the hon. member think that it is a loss of time to take this

vote? I think the hon. member should see his way clear to letting us get along with the Estimates. I am not objecting at all to the vote, but it seems to me a waste of time to take it.

One cannot recognize
without a protest a ruling to the effect that this committee has not entire control of its own proceedings.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext: The hon. member has appealed from the ruling of the Chair, and it remains for me to report the circumstances to the Speaker of the House and for the- House to deal with it. Failing that, there is no discussion to be had on the matter at all.

I appeal from your decision, Mr. Chairman.
The Speaker having resumed the Chair, the Chairman of the Committee reported as follows:
The hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley) having moved that the committee rise, and the Chairman be directed to report to Mr. Speaker that it is not deemed desirable further to consider the Estimates of the Department of Railways and Canals until a reduction has been made in such Estimates by the sum of $1,000,000, I ruled this motion out of order. Against my ruling, the hon. member for St. John appeals to the House.
Ruling confirmed.
The House again in Committee of Supply, Mr. Rhodes in the Chair.
I understood the minister to say that he would build this branch line this year if the Minister of Finance could furnish the money.

I said that while the war was on I would not ask the Minister of Finance for any'money for this railway, but that if the war ceased at any time during the present year, and the Minister of Finance could furnish us the money, we would proceed with it.

It would not be polite, and perhaps not parliamentary, to question the sincerity of my hon. friend, but I should like to remind him that when this Government came into power there was no scarcity of money to build this railway. If I remember rightly, there was about a $30,000,000 surplus at the time this contract was handed over to the present Administration; so it could not have been lack of money that prevented the

[DOT]construction of this branch line
9 p.m. in 1911 and the following years.
The Government at one time decided to strike out this item, and it disappeared from the Estimates for one or two years, but when an election was expected a year or so ago the item reappeared, and I cannot help feeling that its reappearance was a diplomatic move on the part of my hon. friend. Whether he really intends to build the road or not is a question, but judging from the conduct of the administration so far, they are not sincere in their professions about the construction of this line, and I cannot help thinking that the item was put back in the Estimates again, not in order that the road might be built, but for the purpose of influencing votes in that locality. My hon. friend need not think the people interested in this branch line will be convinced by his statement that it is want of money that has prevented its construction. I quite understand that money is not very plentiful at the present time, and I sympathize with the Minister of Finance so far as that is concerned. We have discussed this item several times, and I do not want to take up the time of the House in going over an old story again, but has the line been located?
I understand that the location has been made, and that the plans and profiles are ready.
Does the line touch Mul-grave?
Yes.
What other points on the tidal waters does it touch besides Mul-grave?
I have not the information before me, but the line runs from Sunny-brae to Mulgrave.

The minister has his
officers here. He should be able to give me that information.

I would have to have the
plan or profile to show that, and I have not that here. There will be some other items in the Estimates to be discussed later, and I will give my hon. friend the information he requires before they are passed.

I shall be obliged to
the minister if he will bring his plans and profiles with him, because I wish to obtain
certain information in regard to the exact location of the road.
I will do that.

In answer to an
Order of the House, the minister brought down a return which I have under my hand showing the proposed location of this road.
I am rather surprised to find my hon. friend attempting to delude the people of this country by advancing the idea that, because this item is in the Estimates, if the war is finished between now and next year, he will go on and build this railway. He knows very well that he cannot do anything of the kind; he knows that the financial obligations of the country at the present moment will not permit him to do it; and I fail to see why, knowing that the House knows that to be the case, he undertakes to tell us that. The evidence that the hon. gentleman- will not do anything has been pointed out by the hon. member for Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair). When the Government came into power in 1911 they found that not merely was this road provided for in the Estimates, but all the preliminaries had been arranged, tenders had been called for, and the contract was ready to be signed. My hon. friend and his friends at once proceeded to cut the amount out of the Estimates, and the matter was dropped. It is only now, with rumours of elections, that the minister proceeds to bring this item out of obscurity again and place it in the Estimates. The hon. minister should be frank about the matter, because he knows, as well as he knows anything, that if this war should come to an end in the coming summer, it will be absolutely impossible, in view of the financial obligations of the country, for the Government to undertake the construction of this road. Perhaps the hon. minister is not altogether to blame for deceiving the people as to the building of this road, because last summer, when we were having the doctrine of economy preached everywhere, the hon. gentleman who holds the position of Minister of Railways had troops of surveyors going through the country endeavouring to survey an entirely new line altogether, and one absolutely unnecessary and of no value except for political purposes in the county of Pictou. The people of that county have to-day in operation a branch line from the main line of the Intercolonial between Truro running to'Sunnybrae; but surveyors from my hon. friend's department travelled

through the country for the purpose of duplicating that line with a railway to cost $2,500,000 from Sunnybrae to Kempt Town. If that railway were constructed, the result would be to divert the whole of the trade from the business portion of the county of Pictou, to turn the people of Guysborough away from their natural industries in that county, and to deprive them of the railway connection for which they have long sought. I want to ask my hon. friend, if he has any intention in regard to this matter, if they go so far as to involve the construction of an additional line of railway from Sunnybrae to Mulgrave, and this other line which was proposed by his surveyors, running from Sunpybrae to Kempt Town.

The hon. member states that this Government is bringing this item down just before an election. Of course, hon. gentlemen opposite would not do such a thing; but in this very instance, when the election was on in 1911, they advertised this railway and signed the contract.

You cancelled the
contract.

Yes. But the item was
brought down just before the election was on in Guysborough, for the sole purpose of influencing the people in that constituency.

I wish to correct my hon. ' friend. He will remember that the election preceding that of 1911 took place in 1908; that that meant that only three years of the existing Parliament had expired; that this item was placed in the Estimates at the opening of the session of 1911, early in the session, prior to the reciprocity agreement having been returned from Washington; that the survey had been made with a great deal of care and trouble, and that preparations had been made to construct the road. No person at the time that the item was placed in the Estimates thought that there would not be two years more of the existing Parliament. The reciprocity question had not arisen at the time. Therefore my hon. friend is mistaken in saying that the placing of the item in the Estimates had anything at. all to do with a prospective election. Matters, however, went along a little faster than we expected, and the result wias that during that session the House was dissolved and went to the country. That is the reason why the matter had the' appearance of being an election proceeding; but, as a matter of fact, it was not, and if the

reciprocity question had not come on for decision, the railroad would have been constructed and completed probably before the next election would have been held.
The hon. gentleman states that the item appeared only in the Estimates of 1911.
I siay that, but the Estimates were made up prior to any one expecting an election to occur.

I differ from the hon. member, for this reason. The item was not in the Main Estimates of 1911; but when an election was supposed to be coming on it was brought down in the Supplementary Estimates on the last day of the session, and, that being the case, in my opinion, it was put in there with a view to carrying the hon. member's constituency.
My hon. friend is mistaken in that.

I am giving my understanding. If I am wrong, the hon. member will no douibt bring the matter to my attention again. Even if the item was in the Main Estimates, surely no Government would seriously make a survey for 100 miles of railway before they had any money to spend for surveys or plant until the item bad been passed by Parliament; and when a Government, within a day or two after the dissolution of Parliament, have plans and specifications for a railway made, and have tenders called for and in just before the election, no minister would be justified in awarding a contract. In this case the Minister of Railways, on assuming office, finding that the vote for this line had been passed by Parliament during the session that had closed two or three months prior to his coming into power, cancelled the contract and had a new survey made of the whole situation. Instead of coming down just before the election, he put this item in the Estimates two or three years ago. The only people in Canada who had any idea of an election at that time, so far as I know, were hon. gentlemen opposite. Surely the hon. gentleman did not expect' that we were going to have an election after we had been in power only two years. The facts show that a vote for this line was put in the Estimates in the dying days of the Parliament before the election of 1911, and that within two or three months thereafter tenders were called and contracts awarded. I would not

have mentioned this had not the hon. member for Pictou said that we put this item in the Estimates on account of an election coming on. Hon. gentlemen talk about putting an item in the Estimates just before an election, but I do not think there ever was another case quite equal to this.

My hon. friend is mistaken, as he will find out when he consults the records. On the question of surveys, also, my hon. friend is misinformed. A careful survey was made by the Government of Nova Scotia two years prior to the vote, and the plans and profiles were handed over to the Federal Government, as I understand it. There was no necessity for making another survey. The hon. gentleman must remember that the Musquodoboit road was in exactly the same position. The Government was able to construct that road upon the surveys made .at that time, and there was nothing wrong about them

the road was actually built on those surveys and is running to-day. The hon. gentleman says that this item was placed in the Estimates in 1911 after the late Government had decided to go to the country. But he will remember that no election was decided upon until July, and it must have been very early in the session, when that item was first put in the Estimates.

Even admitting what
the hon. member for Guysborough says, that provision was made for this vote in the winter of 1911, the hon. gentleman will have some difficulty in persuading the people of Nova Scotia that it was not the desire to affect an election that prompted the vote. It is true that it was not generally known that a Dominion election would be held until some two months before polling took place. But there was a provincial election coming on. The Premier of Nova Scotia is a very cautious man and usually "takes the count " before appealing to the people. In 1911, his term of office expired in July, and the election had to come on in the month of June. It was with a view to that election that a great deal of this discussion about the Guysborough road took place. I do not think that my hon. friend from Guysborough will deny that it was a very live issue in the provincial campaign in June. So, even if the recollection of the hon. member is correct and this vote appeared first in the main Estimates instead of in the Supplementary Estimates, its purpose is very evident, particularly to those who knew the history of this movement. As a matter of fact, before every provincial election in Nova Scotia for the last fifteen or twenty years, there has been a very lively agitation for railway construction in this particular vicinity. In the election of 1906, about two weeks before polling day the contractors actually did begin work on the proposed railway. They turned out, I think, with three men and four wheelbarrows to construct the road. I am much pained that hon. gentlemen opposite should raise a protest against this item, particularly my hon. friemd from Pictou (Mr. Macdonald) who represents a county very closely concerned. The good people of Pictou and Guysborough have been fooled and fooled and fooled for many years, in regard to this much-needed road. If there is one part of Nova Scotia that needs railway facilities more than another, it is this part; and I think that the holders of Nova Scotia seats particularly have very little to do to place even a straw in the way of the Minister of Railways carrying out this work. I was pained beyond measure that a gentleman who ought to have concern for the whole klaritime Provinces, the hon. member for St. John (Mr. Pugsley), should deliberately delay this item and move that $1,000,000 be struck off the Estimates of the Minister of Railways and Canals. I can understand that hon. gentlemen opposite may have a desire for economy, may be anxious to curtain expenditures; but did it ever occur to them, I wonder, that a very practical way of economizing at this juncture would be minimizing speech-making? Do hon. gentlemen opposite realize that every day this Parliament is kept in session means added expense to the people of this country? We all enjoy hearing the member for St. John speak; we cannot but admire his flowing periods. But the people of this country are beginning to realize that this is a costly luxury. For every minute that the hon. gentleman speaks, the cost to the country is about $6. In the course of a session that is a considerable amount of money. Let him economize in this way. hut let the people of Guysborough have their railway. I know that the people of Guysborough and Pictou are patriotic; they do not expect to have a railway built while the war is on. They know that every dollar should be appropriated for the all-important task of beating the enemy. But they have the right to expect, and they do expect, that, as soon as the war is over, and our

There is an item here,
$111,000, for a spur line to Courtenay bay. That was voted first in 1912-13, I think. Last year $112,000 was voted, $1,000 was expended, and now the minister is asking for $111,000. What was done under the vote granted in 1912-13?

Nothing has been spent of
the amount voted last year. The amount voted in 1913-14 was $135,000; the amount expended $1,257.35. In 1914-15 the amount voted was $134,000, and the amount expended $2,671.41. The amount voted in 1915-16 was $112,000, and the estimated expenditure during that year $1,000. So we have a revote of $111,000. The construction of the diversion to the Courtenay Bay branch will permit the abandonment of 0.68 miles of the present line, which contains many objectionable street crossings in the city of St. John. The proposed line will be free of all grade crossings and will give the Intercolonial Bailway control of the water front at this point. The amount asked to be revoted will cover the purchase of right of way and all expenses in connection therewith and include preparation of plans. The amount shown does not cover any construction work. The Courtenay bay work, of course, comes under the Public Works Department, and any discussion in connection with it should take place on the Estimates of that department. I have been in St. John only once, and I was around Courtenay bay; I remember the objectionable crossings at that point. The expenditure of this amount will

depend a great deal, I suppose, on how the work proceeds at Courtenay bay.
When was the contract first voted for this work?
It was voted in 1913-14 and in 1914-15; it is now voted again. Practically nothing has been spent, I understand, except a few thousand dollars?
Very little.
Why was the work not proceeded with in 1914?
I really am not in a position to give the hon. member that information. I take it for granted that the Courtenay bay work had not advanced sufficiently.
That would not explain it.

I will get the hon. member
that information

Many items have been
in the Estimates since one or two years before the war broke out and nothing has been done, so that it is no answer to say that these items must remain in the Estimates until the war is over. I make the same remark with regard to the spur at Courtenay bay as I do with regard to the branch line from Sunnybrae to Mulgrave. That amount was in the Estimates of 1911; the Government struck the amount out of the Estimates and then had it in in 1911, 1912, 1913, 1914. During these three years before the war broke out nothing whatever was done towards the building of that branch line. Therefore it will have very little effect with the people who are interested in this line for the hon. member for Annapolis to rise in his place and claim that we are in some way doing injury to the people of that section of Nova Scotia because we criticise the action of the Government in this respect. If any criticism has been made to-night it is of the delay on the part of the Government in proceeding with this necessary work. My motion that the committee rise', and that the Chairman report the views of the committee that $1,000,000 should 'be struck out of the Estimates was .aimed not at any particular item, 'but at all the Estimates of the Department of Eailways and Canals. If that motion had carried it would have meant the reduction of the minister's Estimates by at least $1,000,000. I think there could

well be a reduction of $3,000,000 or $4,000,000, perhaps a little more, without any injury to the public service.
The hon. member will see that the first vote was in the session of 1913-14, and that it was in 1914 that the war broke out, and there were rumours of war probably a month before that.

The year 1913-14 ended on the 31st of March; therefore there would have been ample time to build that road previous to the outbreak of war. The approach to Courtenay bay, at the western side of the peninsula, where the sugar refinery is, and where a large number of wharves are located, is exceedingly dangerous. As the Minister _of Marine and Fisheries knows, the crossings at Haymar-ket square and City road are very dangerous. I am very sorry, indeed, that there has been so much delay in the construction of that sipur; I have never been able to understand why the delay has taken place. I hope the minister will be good enough to look up the papers and get me the information.

I realize that that is a very dangerous spot. I came round there myself one time, from that large piece of property that the Government owns, part of which is now the sugar refinery. The track runs around Courtenay bay right across the streets and near the houses; it is a very dangerous place and should be moved. I assure the hon. member that I will take that up with the management again and see why the delay has occurred -for the amount is not very large. I should ascertain the facts and be able to give them to the hon. member at another sitting.

In that connection, I may say that there is no gate at the crossing of City Road, which is crossed by the present spur; there is no guard there, and, unless some precautions are taken, a dreadful accident will sooner or later occur. The new spur line would do away with the very great danger which exists now.
I am glad the horn member has mentioned that. I will draw attention to the matter.
What i6 the estimated length of the line from Sunnybrae to Mulgrave?

93 miles. For the information of the hon. member for Guysborough,
I may say that I have here the item from the supplementary Estimates for the year ending March 31, 1912, as follows:
Towards the construction of a railway from a point on the Intercolonial railway at or near New Glasgow, in the county of Pictou, (or from Sunnybrae in the said county, in event of the branch line of railway to that place being acquired, as it may be under this appropriation) to the town of Guysborough, and from the said v line of railway at Cross Roads, Country Harbour, to the deep water of the said harbour, ?1,000,000.
When were those Estimates laid before the House?
I have not that information. The hon. gentleman would have to go to Hansard for it.	.
It is stated in this book that the date was March 31. _

No, those were the Estimates for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1912. The supplementary Estimates for the fiscal yeaT 1911-12 were laid before the House a day or two before the House prorogued. Therefore I say that that amount was submitted to Parliament in July, 1911, a day or two before prorogation.

My hon. friend is not
sure of that. There is no evidence of that in the book that he has submitted to me. I would like to know for certain, because I do not think that is true. They were not the final Supplementary Estimates; there were later Supplementary Estimates.

The hon. member knows that the Supplementary Estimates for the fiscal year are always brought down a few days before the House prorogues. The only difference between the hon. member and myself is that I say that the amount was in the Supplementary Estimates, ,and not in the main Estimates. It is a question whether they were brought down in July or a little earlier.
There need be no question about it; we can get at the truth.

Certainly, we can turn up
Hansard and see the date on which the Supplementary Estimates were submitted.

I will look it up and
inform my hon. friend.
I say that- they were not in the main Estimates, but in the Supplementary Estimates.
My recollection is that the particular Supplementary Estimates re-

When Supplementary Estimates are brought down, say for the fiscal year 1911-12, the heading reads:	" Supplementary Estimates for the fiscal year ending 31st March, 1912." But if he looks at those Supplementary Estimates he will see that they were headed, " Further Supplementary Estimates for the year 1911-12," which only proves my point that these Estimates were brought down after the House met in June, 1911. However, we will get the matter settled.
If my hon. friend will refer to the Estimates he has in mind he will find that further supplementary Estimates were brought down-a second supplementary Estimate and a third supplementary Estimate.
It does not make much difference.

It does not make much difference, but when the minister was trying to put over this little job he thought it would ibe interesting to make a digression and talk about what happened in 1911. He was only half right in regard to that, and it is just as well to know the facts. In the Estimates of 1911 two votes were submitted, one providing for the construction of a railway from Dartmouth to Musquodoboit, and the other providing for the construction of a line from Sunnybrae to Muligrave, in the county of Guys'borough, together with the proposition to take over the line of railway from Eureka to Sunnybrae. What took place? My hon. friend, the Acting Minister of Railways and Canals, is an old parliamentarian and a

very astute one, and he knows that he was quibbling. Long before the election of 1911 the Government of the day advertised for tenders in regard to these railways. Tenders were received and contracts for the line of railway from Musquodoboit to Dartmouth were awarded, as were also tenders for a portion of the line from Sunnybrae to Mulgrave, and the line from Sunnybrae to Eureka was taken over by the Government and became part of the Intercolonial. That was in the summer of 1911 and before the election, and there was no possible reason why it should have been taken over-and nobody knows that better than the acting minister himself-unless it was to form part of this extension. If it was not taken over for that purpose it was of no value. The present Government came into office in the autumn of 1911, and what did it do? In the constituency represented by the right hon. the Prime Minister it proceeded to build the line of railway upon an Estimate brought down. It does not make any difference whether it was in the first or second supplementary Estimates. This Government proceeded to build the railway, the contract for which had been let by their predecessors, and the railway is now constructed. That is what was done	in	one case. In the
other case, the case under discussion, they cancelled the contract which had been let by the previous Government, and actually tried to stop the taking o,ver of the line from Eureka to Sunnybrae. I made that statement in this House when the Minister of Railways was present, and he was unable to deny it. From that time to this all that my hon. friend and the Minister of Railways and Canals have done has been to send surveyors cavorting around the country and spending money among party heelers. They have not yet arrived at any conclusion. The survey upon which the contract was let for the road from Musquodoboit to Dartmouth was made by the Provincial Government and adopted by this Government, and the surveys for the line from Sunnybrae to Mulgrave were made in the same way, and tenders were called for on the basis of those surveys. My hon. friend knows that because one county was represented by the Prime Minister and the other by my hon. friend from Guysborough, the one got the railway and the other did not. Last year when the country was said to be calling in thunder tones for an election, my hon. friend put in the Estimates a vote for a

million dollars ill connection with this railway. The Government, knew very well when they put that vote in the Estimates that the condition of the finances of the country would not permit of the construction of the railway, and they know that to-day. It does strike me as peculiar that an hon. gentleman who has been so long in Parliament as my hon. friend, should have the audacity to come before this House and think that he can foil the people with the ridiculous pretence that this railway would be built this year if the war stopped. He knows that it is not so, and when he makes that statement to the House he knows it is not true. That is the situation with regard to the matter -and these are the facts. They cannot be questioned. Everybody know? that the Government is not going to build this line this y6ar, and the minister knows it. We have here an item for $978,000. What has become of the $22,000, the difference between that amount and the $1,000,000 which was voted last year? That is a question which I hope the acting minister will answer.
Carried.

My hon. friend will not succeed in getting this item carried by 'remarks of that kind; he will probably find that he will only prolong- the discussion. It is just as well that we should understand where we are in regard to this matter. Last year, while the Minister of Finance was talking economy, and all this hypocrisy was being paraded before the people of this country, my hon. friend and the Minister of Railways and Canals kept chasing up and down that part of the country corps of Surveyors fed by party heelers, and money was being spent gratuitously to help out the party. According to the return which I have here, this railway was to be 93 miles long, and it was to cost $51,200 per mile. The total cost was to be $4,653,060. Does any one believe that this Government is going to embark this year on an expenditure of $4,653,000, even if the war should stop next month? But they were not content with that hypocrisy. This return contains the report made to the engineer of construction in regard to another railway. I have already stated that the original proposal in regard to this matter involved the taking over of a line of railway from Eureka to Sunnybrae which is part of the Intercolonial railway. The
result is that traffic is now being carried on to Sunnybrae.
Is the line from Eureka to Sunnybrae about nine miles long?

Yes, it is part of the Intercolonial which is being operated. The hon. gentleman, notwithstanding his pretence of economy, proposes to continue the farce of keeping a band of surveyors travelling around the country to survey this line of railway that would parallel the line from Sunnybrae to Eureka. So we have a report dated November 15, 1915, on a projected line from Sunnybrae to Glengarry, which is as follows:
Projected location 0*6 per cent compensated grade-Sunnybrae to Glengarry.
Under this date are returned to you plan, profile and estimate. This is part of the Sunny-brae-Kempt Town proposed line. It connects at Sunnybrae with the 1915 location Mulgrave-Sunnybrae. The present returns include the adopted portions of several alternative routes which have been reported on, the latest revised projection and through chainage and mileage from Sunnybrae to Glengarry. At the latter place iit connects with the Glengarry-Kempt-Town projected location, separate returns for which are being made.
This- line is intended to carry the through traffic of the Mulgrave-Sunnybrae line which would otherwise have to be carried over the Sunnybrae subdivision to Perrona Junction, and thence over Mulgrave subdivision at increased distance, and requiring extensive grade revisions, as has been noted in reconnaisance reports. The country traversed is served indirectly by present lines, and any increase in local traffic offering would he due to increased facility in reaching the railroad.
That report is signed by L. H. Robinson, assistant engineer, and it is addressed to the enginer of construction, Moncton, N.B. The effect of this proposal which the department are making is that, through a new country from Sunnybrae to Glengarry, they propose to build a line of railway duplicating the existing line, a nice proposal to make when we have a debt of $800,000,000 or $900,000,000. The cost of this proposal, in addition to the $4,000,000 that I have already outlined, according to this estimate is $2,053,925. My hon. friend's proposal in regard to this matter involves a cost of something like $6,000,000. He has the nerve to ask this House and the country to suppose that he and his Government are going to be in a position to embark upon a $6,000,000 expenditure even if the war stops this year, more particularly in regard to this proposition costing $2,000,000 from Sunnybrae to Glengarry because my hon. friend is there going to

build an entirely unnecessary and unjustifiable piece of road. In the report the suggestion is made to build a tunnel through the mountains which will cost a large sum of money. This is an absolutely unnecessary and unjustifiable undertaking, the result of which would be that instead of the constituency of my hon. friend from Guysborough (Mr. Sinclair) 'being kept in ' touch with the industrial centres of eastern Nova Scotia, the minister is going to spend $2,000,000 to take the business away. He would deprive these industrial towns of the business which would naturally centre there on account of the construction of this new line. He would deprive New Glasgow' and Stellarton of their railway facilities and workshops and the advantages which they enjoy as railway centres. He would impose an expense upon the country which would be entirely unnecessary and unjustifiable and he would destroy existing conditions and discriminate against the industrial centres in eastern Nova Scotia. I want to know if my hon. friend intends to include as part of this Sunnyibrae line the extension from Sunnybrae to Glengarry. Is that part of the scheme which is to be initiated as a result of this vote? Does my hon. friend intend to carry out as part of his scheme of railway construction this totally unnecessary line of railway and to take away the traffic from these industrial centres as a natural consequence of this vote? Does he intend the Sunny-brae-Kempt Town line to be part of the' Sunnybrae-Mulgrave line?

There are several points that the hon. gentleman raised that I will touen upon as I go along. In the first place, the hon. member, I think from the way he made the statement, would lead the committee to believe that the Minister of Railways took over the Eureka branch-
No, the late Government did that.
Yes, I was going to say that. The hon. member knows that the nine miles was taken over between nomination and election in 1911.
Not at all.
That is the information I have.
They were working at it for months and months.
Finally it was taken over.
They started searching the title in July.

But the title was completed at that time, and that portion of the railway was taken over by the late Government. There has been quite a lot said about plans. The local Government made the plans, and tenders were called. The local Government handed over the plans to the Dominion Government, and, of course, the Dominion Government having had the plans, we had to contract on the plans that weTe made by the local Government. The plans in connection with this railway were not handed over to the Dominion Government until 1912. My hon. friend the Minister of Railways and Canals took these plans from the local Government in that year. Therefore, if tenders were called on these plans, they were not then really the property of the Dominion Government.

How does my hon.
friend explain the Musquodoboit railway and the fact that the plans were prepared prior to the date of the vote? Were they* not prepared when this vote was brought down?
I am talking about the Sunnybrae road.

But these two roads went together, they were voted together, contracted for together, and they were expected to be built together. My .hon. friend found the Musquodoboit railway in such a forward condition that 'he was able to take it over without making any new plan. Why not the Sunnybrae line?
The Musquodoboit railway plans were taken over from the local Government and the work was proceeded with, but it had to be gone over again after the plans were taken over by the department.
What is the point about these plans?
Some Ron. members stated that the Dominion Government had the plans ready before the contract was awarded and prior to the present Government coming into power.
I stated that the local Government had made a very thorough survey a couple of years before this vote was taken.
My point is that those plans were not in the possession of the Dominion Government.
How were the tenders called for?
I do not know. The minister had to send his officials and take over the plans in 1912.

The minister is misinformed. I saw the plans in the Railway office with my .own eyes, prior to the time this Estimate was brought down; very complete plans they were, too, showing the location of the Sunnybrae line all the way from Sunnybrae to Guysborough. There were some little difficulties at the west end that had not been settled, but the plans were there, and tenders had been asked for.

The plans may have been
there, but full details were not in the Railway Department.

Just as good plans
for the Sunnybrae road as for the Dartmouth road.

I am surry to see my hon.
friend from Pictou opposing this vote. Apparently he does not want us to build this road.

The minister and I
are both old parliamentarians and he need not begin that kind of tactics with me. I do not want that kind of thing, and my hon. friend might as well drop it right away. I am directly charging the minister with an attempt to deceive the House and the country by putting a vote in these Estimates when he knows he is not going to use a single dollar of it on construction this year.	*
I thought the hon. member was opposing the vote altogether. I cannot make any stronger statement than I have made with regard to the action of the department in this matter.
You know that what I am saying is correct.

If the minister will allow me to speak on a matter which, perhaps, it would have been better to bring up on a Levis item, I should like to draw his attention to certain damages that were caused at Levis some years ago, by the sparks from an engine of the Intercolonial. In order to refresh the memory of the'deputy
minister, whom I see sitting beside my hon friend, I will read the following questions which were asked on the 8th of June, 1915, by the hon. member for Levis, Mr. Bour-assa:
1.	Is there before the Government a report on the destruction of Mr. T. Paradis' sawmill and lumber yard at LSvis, P.Q. ?-A. Yes.
2.	Did the Government appoint a commissioner to report on that fire?-A. Yes.
3.	Who was the commissioner, and what did he report?-A. L. A. Audette. That the fire which destroyed the mill of Telesphore Paradis, at L,dvis, in the province of Quebec, on the 19th day of July, 1906, was, in his opinion, caused by sparks from a locomotive of the Intercolonial railway.
4.	What is the reason the Government does
not act upon the commissioner's report?-A. No amount for damages by said loss has been agreed upon.	.
5.	How much does the Department of Railways and Canals value Mr. Paradis' alleged damages at?-A. The department does not deem it advisable to state the estimate of the valuation of the loss while the matter remains in the present condition.
6 What is the reason Mr. Paradis' claim has not yet been settled?-A. Answered by No. 4.
Let me state briefly the facts of the case. First of all, I hold no brief from Mr. Paradis. He is an old political friend of the party at present in power, a well known gentleman of the Quebec district, who has been engaged in lumbering operations for the last fifty years. He is a highly respected lumberman of the old French-Canadian type. One evening on the 11th of July, 1906, a fire caused by the sparks from an engine of, I ibelieve, the Maritime express completely destroyed not only his mills and machinery, but also a wharf which he owned at Levis. Some time afterwards the old gentleman instituted proceedings in the Exchequer Court of Canada, and while his case was before the court a judgment was rendered by the Supreme Court in the case of Chamberlain vs. the King, reported in the Supreme Court Reports, Volume 42, p. 350. In that case it was decided that to succeed the claimant's property had to be situated on the " Public Work "-on the right of way of the Intercolonial railway- a somewhat anomalous conclusion, which brought the following remarks from one of the judges:
With the policy of Parliament we have nothing to do. Our duty is simply to construe the language of the Act, and if that construction does not fully carry out the intention of Parliament, and if a wider and broader jurisdiction is desired to be given, the Act can easily be amended.
Now, this decision, which was given on appeal on October 20, 1909, actually put

Paradis out of court, but the Act in question was amended on April 8, 1910, by 9 Edward VII, Chapter 19, giving the Exchequer Court wider jurisdiction. If the poor old gentleman-he was a well-to-do business man until the fire, but that left him in rather poor oircum-
10	p.m. stances-had instituted proceedings under the Act as amended, he would have succeeded in his claim, but the new Act, unlike the taxation measures of the Minister of Finance, had no retroactive feature, and Mr. Paradis had to abandon his action as being out of court. He had only a moral claim against the department, and he was .left to the tender mercies of the old Government and of the present Government. I remember having seen him on several occasions in Ottawa, and it was rather a pitiable sight to see the venerable old gentleman absolutely ruined by that fire, and deprived, by one of those glorious uncertainties of the law, of all recourse against his majesty. I may say, however, that the present Government, on being remonstrated with and appealed to, decided at last to appoint a commissioner to investigate the causes of the fire, because at first it had been denied that the fire had been caused by the sparks from one of the locomotives of the Intercolonial railway. I have here the Order in Council appointing the commission, but I do not think it necessary to read it.
No, I remember the case quite well.	-

Mr. Justice Audette- and no better judge could be selected- was appointed as commissioner; he investigated the case, and, after having visited the place and having heard many witnesses, he made to the department a long report, in which he properly weighed the credibility of all the witnesses, and came to the conclusion that unquestionably the fire was caused by sparks emitted by a locomotive passing at about one o'clock in the morning, and that that fire had destroyed the buildings and property belonging to the claimant. Of course, the commissioner was not empowered to assess the. value of the buildings, nor to do anything but fix the responsibility for the fire, and the conclusion is that the responsibility rests with the Government. I make a strong appeal to the spirit of fair play of the hon. minister. As the judge of the Exchequer Court, the commissioner in this case, states very plainly in his report, if Mr. Paradis had instituted the proceedings after the judg-
[Mr. Lemleuxl
ment rendered by the Supreme Court, and after the Exchequer Court Act had been amended by the Parliament of Canada, he would certainly have succeeded, but he was the victim of the deficiencies of the law, and the judges on the bench criticised the law as it had been framed. Now that the Government is aware that Mr. Paradis was morally right in claiming from the Government the damages which he claimed, cannot the Government come to terms with him? As I have stated, the old gentleman is not a political friend of mine, but he is a friend of all those who come into contact with him. He is a gentleman of the old type, one of those who are to-day altogether too rare. I met him not very long ago and I said: " Are you still after [DOT]your claim?" " Well," he said, "I have lost nearly all hope, but certainly it seems to me that the 'Government ought to settle it." You have the Act which has been amended; you have the report of the commissioner, stating that the responsibility rests with the Government, that the fire was caused by sparks emitted by' one of tho locomotives of the Intercolonial raliway. Now the Government has only to say one more word or to proceed one step further, and it will satisfy this old gentleman, who is about to leave the world. In fact, I think Mr. Paradis is about seventy-five or seventy-seven years of age.
He is seventy-eight.

Mr. Paradis had a splendid business; he was a member of the Board of Trade of Quebec; he has been reeve of the county of Lievis; he has on several occasions been asked to run as a candidate for this House, but he preferred to stay in business and did not enter the political arena. Let my hon friend look into the record, and, if die finds the facts as I have stated them to be correct, let him come to terms with Mir. Paradis. I am told, although I am not sure, that the old gentleman was offered an amount, but it was infinitesimal. I am quite sure that if any fair or reasonable offer is made to Mr. Paradis, his family will induce him to accept it. I leave the case with my hon. friend. I wanted to relate the facts just to refresh his memory and in order to give him an opportunity to do a good turn to a citizen who has a rightful claim against the Crown.

(Translation.) Mr. Chairman, I am with one of the hon. member

for Rouville (Mi-. Lemieux) in liis expressions of sympathy relative to Mr. Paradis, who has suffered .severely through a fire started by a spark from a locomotive on the Intercolonial. I think I know how the fire started, anl I would be 'highly gratified if the hon. Minister of Railways could see his way to helping that gentleman. I trust' the minister will find some effective means of compensating that poor man for the losses incurred.
Mr. TURGEON-I am very well pleased that the hon. member for Rouville has drawn the attention of the House to that old claim of Mr. Paradis of Levis. He has stated the claim better than I can state it myself, especially so far as the law is concerned. I know the particulars of the case as far as any layman can know them. I know also the extent of the loss that this man has suffered, and I am aware that the department two or three years ago made him a small offer which he could not accept. I have seen the report of Mr. Justice Au-dette, the commissioner appointed to state whether or not the department was responsible for Mr. Paradis' loss by fire. Judge Audette, after taking full evidence, more than had been given before the Court of Exchequer, stated that there was not the least doubt that the department was responsible for setting the fire, as the fire originated through a defective system on the Intercolonial. I think the department acknowledged its responsibility by making an offer to Mr. Paradis, but it was too small according to that gentleman's estimate. So, he is asking the department to appoint a commissioner to assess the damage caused by the fire. When I was informed that the matter had been referred to Judge Audette, I was under the impression that he was empowered to estimate the loss, but, as the hon. member for Rouville has stated, Judge Audette was not allowed to do .more than to.state the cause of the loss. But, as it is clear that the department is responsible for causing the fire, I think a commissioner should be appointed, as requested, to assess the loss. I think it would be easy to come to an understanding, and I am confident that no member of the House would find fault with the decision of such a'commission.

I know a little about this claim, but, of course, not so much as the hon. minister himself. The case, as I understand it, stands in this way: a fire took place which destroyed Mr. Paradis'
property, and he laid a claim against the Government. The Minister of Railways of that time, the hon. member for South Renfrew (Mr. Graham), as is usual in such cases, referred the matter to the Exchequer Court. The decision of the court was, as the hon. member for Rouville has stated and Mr. Paradis lost his case.	.
The court held that it could not try the case.

At all. events, the decision of the court was that it had not full jurisdiction to proceed with the case. When we came into power, Mr. Paradis urged the present minister, Mr. Cochrane, to deal with the matter.	As to Mr. Paradis himself, I have met the old gentleman several times, and I agree with every word that the hon. member for Rouville has said. No finer old gentleman have I ever met than Mr. Paradis. I sympathize with him very much in his loss, and feel that he is deserving of consideration, even though it was decided that he could not recover under the law, as it stood at that time. Not being able to have the case disposed of through the courts, the Minister of Railways and Canals appointed Judge Audette to ascertain whether the fire originated in the way alleged or not. The report of Judge Audette has been read. The Minister of Railways and Canals, I think hon. members will agree, sympathized deeply with Mr. Paradis in his loss; otherwise, he would not have gone even as far as he did. He never realized that the claim of Mr. Paradis might make up such an amount as it did. If I remember correctly -and I have only my memory to trust to in this matter-Judge Audette decided, after hearing evidence, that the fire was started by a locomotive. Mr. Paradis asked the minister to pay him the amount of the loss, and the Minister of Railways, being anxious to come to some terms that would help Mr. Paradis in his great loss, offered him, I think, $10,000. Afterwards he offered him $13,000. I was acting for the Minister of Railways when he was in England, and I remember very well that appeal was made to* me to deal with the case. I was informed by the officials of the department that the Minister of Railways and Canals was making what seemed a reasonable offer, taking all the circumstances into consideration. If I remember well, Mr. Paradis claimed $56,000. Of course, I was only acting minister, but I was anxious to get the case settled, and so I made an offer

of $15,000-that is, I advanced the offeT $2,000, and, I was willing, and still am willing, to carry out that offer. I felt that for one in my position as acting minister, that was dealing very fairly with Mr. Paradis, after what had taken place up to that time. But Mr. Paradis would not accept tlxat amount, and so I had to ask him to wait until the minister himself returned. I cannot say what has taken place since that time. I was exceedingly anxious to get the matter closed up, and even if the minister had been here at the time, and I know that the Minister of Railways felt very well disposed towards Mr. Paradis. But the difference between Mr. Paradis and the department is so great, and, as it will be necessary, I presume, to ask Parliament to vote whatever sum is decided upon, I thought that the offer of $2,000 more than the minister had offered was a reasonable advance to be made by one in my position.

What has occurred
since?

I do not think I ever spoke to the Minister of Railways and Canals about the matter. But I would have carried out the order I have made, and am ready to carry it out to-day. I am sure that the Minister of Railways and Canals will be glad to carry out anything I say in the matter. I could not tell the hon. member whether Mr. Paradis saw the minister after that date; at any rate, that is the way the matter stands. I was certainly only too anxious to help Mr. Paradis out. I think the hon. member will agree that the fact that he was offered $15,000 shows that the minister had a kindly feeling in the matter.

I shall certainly bring
the attention of Mr. Paradis, when I see him, to the very kind remarks made by the acting minister.
I only mention that because I was under the impression that the hon. member did not know that any substantial offer had been made.

I was informed that a very small amount had been offered. I do not know the circumstances of this case well enough to say that Mr. Paradis was not justified in demanding a larger amount than that which was offered, but from the little that I know about the matter the offer made by the minister seems to be very fair, and I shall certainly call the attention of Mr. Paradis to that.

I want the hon. member to
say also to Mr. Paradis that I feel very sorry for him. I agree with every word the hon. member has said with regard to Mr. Paradis; he is one of the finest old gentlemen that I have ever met, and my heart was with him to do all I could. But, in a matter like this-he was out of court, as it were-I thought the offer made was fair.

The kind words of the
acting minister have convinced me that he should at once appoint a commissioner to make a valuation of the damage caused by the fire. As to the amount of $15,000, I have heard it mentioned before. I mentioned the matter to the Minister of Railways and Canals two years ago, and at that time he told me that he had offered Mr. Paradis about $12,000. The minister said also that he would be willing to add a few thousand dollars to that in order to effect a settlement. I happen to be related to Mr. Paradis; I am a cousin bf his. As the hon. member for Rouville says, he is a very good Conservative, and I have not been able during the last twenty years to convert him to the Liberal party, not even since his recent lose, which he attributes to the Conservative Government. I happened to visit Mr. Paradis a month or two before the fire, and I have since felt impressed that if anything that I saw there was destroyed by fire, $15,000 would certainly not cover half or, perhaps, one-quarter of the loss. I am inclined to believe that the $50,000 or $60,000 that Mr. Paradis claims is very near the amount of his loss. Of course, my knowledge is superficial. I do suggest that the acting minister should appoint a commissioner to ascertain the damage done by the fire. I do not believe that Mr. Paradis will accept $15,000 to-day any more than he did two years ago or a month or two ago when he was here last. However, I am thankful to the member for Rouville and to the Acting Minister of Railways for what they have said. I hope that the acting minister will put into concrete form the sentiments that he has expressed on behalf of Mr. Paradis.

A short time ago I moved for a return in regard to a proposed new bridge across the harbour of Pictou. The 'bridge which has been there for a long time is getting old and requires to be renewed. There has been under consideration for some time the construction of a new bridge crossing the harbour lower

down and completing what is known as the short line by giving close connection with New Glasgow and eastern Nova Scotia. I find in this return that another suggestion has been made in regard to the matter. The following is a memorandum dated December 2, 1915, from Mr. Brown, chief engineer,, to Mr. Gutelius:
The present Pictou harbour bridge between Loch Broom and Brown's Point on the line from Stellarton to Piotou and Oxford Junction (known as the short line) is about 4,000 feet long and consists of a through steel span and a draw span on pile foundations, the balance of the structure being pile bridge. The majority of piles in this structure are over 60 feet long, which length is necessary on account of the great depth of the mud at this point.
Extensive repairs have tbeen put on this structure in the past two or three years in order to maintain it until the question of grade revision east of Moncton was settled. The bridge is now in such a condition that it requires entire renewal. -
From the data which has been gathered it appears that this bridge will never become a part of the future low grade line, and owing to the high cost of construction of a new permanent bridge, which will run anywhere from $400,000 to $1,000,000 and to the high maintenance cost of such a large structure, it is recommended that a diversion of the line between Stellarton and Pictou be made around the western side of Pictou harbour. From a reconnaissance report which I now have it is estimated that this diversion can be made for approximately $400,000 on grades not exceeding those on the present short line. This diversion will increase the length by about five miles between Pictou and Stellarton, but will not materially affect the distance- between Stellarton or Pictou and Oxford Junction,
I also find in the return a formal recommendation signed by Mr. McGowan for an appropriation of $400,000 to cover the cost of construction of a diversion of the line between Stellarton, N.S., and Pictou, N.S., around the western side of Pictou harbour, so as to eliminate the reconstruction of Pictou harbour bridge. The recommendation says that survey is now being made, and gives the following as the necessity for the proposed work:
The existing bridge across Pictou harbour requires complete renewal. The cost of replacing same with a permanent bridge may run to $1,000,000, which will be greatly in excess of the cost of the diversion r.commended.
I hope that the acting minister will not proceed to spend any money in constructing a diversion of line such as is recommended here. A short time ago I referred to what was called the Sunnybrae and Kemptown line. I cannot conceive of that line being considered at all, unless for the purpose of diverting the through traffic between Sydney and Moncton down to Truro
instead of utilizing what has always been known as the short line, which was built by Sir Charles Tupper when he was Minister of Railways for the avowed purpose of establishing a line of railway which would give the shortest possible communication on the Intercolonial with Sydney and other eastern points. The bridge which at present crosses the harbour is old, but I think it can be repaired. The Liberal Government had in view the construction of this bridge across the harbour; I understand also that it was the view of the present minister that it should be proceeded with. I want to ask the acting minister not to proceed with the diversion; if he did, it would prevent the building of the bridge. I quite recognize the financial situation, but in my judgment the construction of that bridge would be an immense advantage to railway operation in eastern Nova Scotia-and the bridge and the bridge only should be built. The diversion would be a great blow to Pictou and eastern Nova Scotia, while the bridge would be the culmination of the short line connection between Oxford Junction and New Glasgow, and would enable the Railway Department to operate by the shortest* and most satisfactory route from Sydney to Moncton. It would appear as if an appropriation might be included in the Supplementary Estimates, but I think I voice the opinion of the people in my constituency when I suggest to the minister that no steps be taken to change the existing conditions until the world rights itself again, and the matter can be dealt with in a proper way. Any hasty or ill-considered action would penalize the people interested for all time to come, and would prevent the consummation of what has long been the aspiration of the people in that vicinity, the building of that bridge, and the consummation of a line of railway which would connect Sydney and New Glasgow and the coal and iron districts of Nova Scotia by the shortest route possible, not only with Moncton, but with all points west. 'Speaking in the interests of the people affected, and in the interests of the railway and of the country, I would therefore ask the minister to retain existing conditions until we are in a position to enable us to proceed with the work in a proper way and construct the 'bridge.

This is a very important matter, and one that requires a very great deal of eare before arriving at a final decision. In discussing it with Mr. Gutelius some



time ago, I understood that he had surveyors down there during the past year looking over the situation with the view of having it before him in the event of the minister deciding to go on with the work. But there is nothing in this Estimate for that work, and it is not the intention of th$ department to go on with any work of a permanent character during the present year, so far as changing the route ot building a new bridge is concerned. We may repair the old bridge, or do some work of that kind, but there is nothing in the Estimates'-
And there will not be?
And there will not be this year.

Reverting to the Guys-borough road, I am able to give the minister the correct date when the Estimate was submitted in 1911. The minister threw out an insinuation, which I do not think he intended ill ctt tlio Icite Government put $1,000,000 in the Estimates for this railway for political purposes. I questioned that statement, and pointed out to him that the matter was dealt with* before there was any idea of an election in 1911.. On looking up the Votes and Proceedings I find that the Estimate was submitted to the House on the 17th of May, 1911, and that on the 19th of May, two days later, $416,000 of the amount was voted.

When that estimate
was submitted, was there not a provincial campaign in progress?

It had nothing whatever to do with ,a Provincial campaign. We have listened for about three hours to matters concerning the construction of railways, and now for a few minutes I wish to speak about the destruction of railways. Some thirty years ago a railway was constructed between Chatham and Fredericton. In order that members of the committee may follow me, let me briefly give the history of the line in question. The Intercolonial trunk line was opened in 1875, and soon after-
11	p.m. wards a branch line was built from Chatham to tap the main line at Chatham Junction. A few years later a project was brought forward for the construction of a line from Chatham Junction to Fredericton.
A charter was granted by the provincial Government for the construction of this line. There was some difference of opinion as to where it should tap the main line. The Hon. Peter Mitchell, then the respected member for my county in the House of Commons, strongly urged upon the Government that the line should tap the main line on the north side of the southwest branch of the Miramichi river at Derby Junction. The charterers, however, who got the right to construct the railway, instead of building it to tap the main line on the north side of the river, decided to construct it to tap tihe main line at Chatham Junction and thus* connect with the railway that ran into Chatham. That proposition was opposed by the Hon. Peter
Mitchell, who was able to induce the Dominion Government to build a short line from Derby Junction, some twelve miles up the river on the north side to what is known as Indiantown, and this was operated by the Railway Department for a number of years and known as the Indiantown branch of the Intercolonial, the train leaving Newcastle every evening and returning .to Newcastle the following morning. About the same time the line was completed from Fredericton to Chatham Junction, and then it was amalgamated with the line from Chatham Junction into Chatham, and eventually was known as the Canada Eastern railway owned by 'the Alexander Gibson Manufacturing Company. The road was later on extended on to Loggieville and a loop or diversion was made by Nelson.
About twelve years ago the Dominion Government purchased this line from the Alexander Gibson Manufacturing Company for in round figures about three-quarters of a million dollars, and undertook the operation of the line between Fredericton and Loggieville on the south side of the Miramichi river. The Government had all along operated a short line on the north side of the river. After the Government purchased this road from the Alexander Gibson Manufacturing Company, they put in working order a missing link of some five miles between Blackville and Indiantown. and so they operated the road from Newcastle to Blackville instead of to Indiantown. The committee will understand that the road operated into Chatham runs down	on the	south	side of the
river.	What I assert is that . residents on the south side of the river had. rights and privileges that no person could lightly take away from them. Their farms were taken and segregated. They received, it may be true, a small pittance for the right of way through their farms. This may have been paid or it may not, because, if the owner did not in a very short time accept the offer, his. claim went out of date, and I am not sure * whether they all received the pittance for the right of way or not. At any rate, their farms were segregated; the road was constructed and was operated for some thirty years, and the Government then came to the conclusion that they would not operate a portion of the line, that is to say, the line between Blackville and Chatham Junction, namely, sixteen miles. Instead of operating their line on the south side of the river, they

decided to run all their trains down the north side of the river and to take up the rails on the south side of the river, thus leaving the roadbed without rails and the residents without . the railway privileges that they had enjoyed, nay, more, that they had paid for, because the local government which granted the charter for this road subsidized it and the money of these residents went into the construction of that piece of railway. If a railway corporation owned the railway on each side of the river, the one being 'only 16 miles long and other 125 miles between Fredericton and Loggie-ville, and they said to the Railway Commission: "We want to cease operating that piece of road on the south side of the river," what would the Railway Commission say? They would say: " These people have vested rights, and you must not take away from them the railway privileges that they have paid for and that they have enjoyed for upwards of a quarter of a century." Now, I have said that if these two pieces of road were owned by a railway corporation, the Crown would step in and interfere with any attempt on their part to cease operating a portion of the railway on either side of the river. Yet, on the .principle that the King can do no harm, and that the King will not allow any ohe else to do any harm, what does the King do? The King steps in and robs one hundred people of their vested rights.
Who acts for the King?
